title: Indubitability, Self-Intimating States, and Logically Privileged Access
The Nature and Reach of Privileged Access

items.abstract: Two ideas have played a prominent role in philosophical discussions of self-knowledge. The first is the idea that we enjoy introspective ways of finding out about ourselves are fundamentally different from our ways of finding out about ordinary physical objects and other psychological subjects. The second is the idea (Hume’s elusiveness thesis) that when we find out about our own properties through introspection we are not acquainted with any object whose properties they are. It is natural to think that these two ideas are related – and, in particular, that it is (at least partly) because we do not encounter the self as an object in introspection that the knowledge of the self gained through introspection is epistemically privileged. This paper explores this idea in the context of awareness of one’s own body in proprioception and in ordinary perceptual awareness.
title: The Elusiveness Thesis, Immunity to Error through Misidentification, and Privileged Access

items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Williamson’s anti-luminosity argument has been thought to be in tension with the doctrine that we enjoy privileged epistemic access to our own mental states. In this chapter, it will be argued that the tension is only apparent. Friends of privileged access who accept the conclusion of the argument need not give up the claim that our beliefs about our own mental states are mostly or invariably right, nor the view that mental states are epistemically available to us in a way that renders everything within our mind ‘open to view’—arguably, two main pillars of their doctrine. What they need to reject is the idea that the mental is a realm whose ‘determinacy’ or ‘fineness of grain’ never escapes our appreciation. This idea—it will be suggested—is not essential to privileged access, and defenders of the doctrine should not be afraid to give it up.</jats:p>
title: Privileged Access Without Luminosity

items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
               <jats:p>This chapter provides an overview of some of the main developments in the use of introspective methods in early experimental psychology (mainly 1860-1920). During this period, a key concern about introspective methods was the problem of self-observation, namely that introspecting experience distorts or destroys the target experience. It was raised prominently by Auguste Comte and dominated methodological discussion among so-called ‘introspectionist psychologists’. The chapter applies the proposed framework to set out the flow of this debate among some of the main figures in early psychology, presenting their responses to the problem of self-observation. Doing so makes clear that one of the most salient differences among the different responses is the appeal to different modes of introspective access and how these are best exploited in an empirical investigation of the mind. This shows the value both of the book’s proposed framework and of the insights of the early psychologists.</jats:p>
title: The Problem of Self-Observation

title: The Elusiveness Thesis, Immunity to Error through Misidentification, and Privileged Access

items.abstract: Children are prone to similar errors in attributing beliefs (or belief-based emotions) to themselves or to another person. Children also display no obvious advantage or accuracy in talking about their own mental states compared with those of other people. By implication, children have no special access to their own mental states. However, a closer examination of children’s reference to knowing and not knowing, shows that they talk asymmetrically about their own knowledge as compared with that of an interlocutor. More specifically, young children—two-year-olds—ask questions about what others know but not about what they know themselves. Conversely, they deny that they have knowledge but rarely deny that others have knowledge. The data imply that children have privileged access to, and less uncertainty about, their own knowledge states as compared with those of other people. Potential implications for future research on children’s developing theory of mind are discussed.
title: Revisiting privileged access
Language facilitates introspection: Verbal mind-wandering has privileged access to consciousness

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
               <jats:p>This chapter looks in detail at each of the different modes of introspective access at the centre of the proposed framework: inner attention, inner apprehension, and retrospection. They are characterised according to sets of core features which express available common ground among different theorists who recognise (any or all of) these modes of introspective access in some manner. Doing so makes clear just how different our basic pictures of these modes of introspective access are. There are differences not just in terms of the specific types of features attributed, but also in terms of how developed each basic picture is. Inner attention is the most, while retrospection the least detailed. Another difference concerns how amenable each basic picture is to connect with empirical psychology, and which areas of scientific research might be relevant.</jats:p>
